A Hindu asked a muslim - Why the Muslim rulers were killing the Hindus? (Fictional Story from Finland)
It was a chilly spring afternoon in Tampere, but the Tampere University student cafeteria was buzzing with warm conversations and the clinking of cutlery. As usual, Umar and Arun Kumar, both second-year students in Automation Engineering, had found a quiet spot in the corner to have lunch together.
They had become close friends over the past year — sharing jokes, working on class projects, and learning from each other’s cultures. But today, something was off.
Umar noticed it immediately.
"Hey Arun, you alright?" Umar asked, looking up from his tray of rice and vegetables. "You seem quiet. Your face looks a bit tense.”
Arun hesitated for a second, then sighed. “Yeah… something’s bothering me. I wasn’t sure if I should say it.”
“Go ahead, bro. I’m listening,” Umar said calmly.
Arun shifted uncomfortably. “Last night, I watched this Indian historical movie — Chhaava. It shows how Aurangzeb, the Mughal emperor, captured and brutally killed Shambaji, the son of Shivaji. It really disturbed me… I mean, those scenes, the cruelty… I couldn’t sleep.”
Umar listened attentively.
“And?” he asked gently.
“I don’t know, Umar. It made me feel… angry. Like, why did Muslim rulers do that to Hindus?”
Umar nodded slowly. He understood where Arun’s feelings were coming from. And more importantly, he knew this was a moment that required patience, not defensiveness.
“I’m really sorry you felt that way, Arun,” Umar said sincerely. “That must’ve been heavy. But can I share something with you, as a friend?”
Arun nodded.
“First of all,” Umar began, “what you saw in the movie is one version of history — maybe accurate, maybe exaggerated. History is complicated, and it’s often written from a certain perspective. Every side tends to show their version in the best light, and their enemies in the worst. We have to be careful not to judge entire communities based on one version of history.”
Arun leaned in, listening more intently now.
“Secondly,” Umar continued, “just because someone was a Muslim ruler doesn’t mean he acted according to Islam. Islam doesn’t allow cruelty or injustice — not even towards animals, let alone humans. If any ruler, whether Muslim or not, committed injustice, Islam doesn't approve of that.”
Arun frowned slightly. “But what about Aurangzeb?”
Umar nodded. “Good question. There are actually historians who say different things about Aurangzeb. Some portray him as a devout and just ruler, others criticize him for being harsh. The truth is — we weren’t there. We can't be 100% sure of everything that happened.”
He paused, then added, “But even if some of the negative stories are true — we as Muslims don’t take Aurangzeb as our role model. Our example is the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his companions, who treated even their enemies with mercy.”
Arun seemed thoughtful. “Hmm... I didn’t know that. I thought Muslims looked up to all the Mughal rulers.”
“Not at all,” Umar replied. “The early caliphs of Islam, like Caliph Umar ibn Al-Khattab, ruled vast empires, but Christians and Jews lived peacefully under their rule. They had rights, safety, and freedom of worship. That’s the Islamic model of governance — not tyranny.”
He continued, “And think about this — if Aurangzeb really wanted to kill all Hindus, would there be so many Hindus still in India today? Why were there Hindu generals under his rule? Why didn’t he kill them?”
Arun blinked. “You’re saying the wars were about power, not religion?”
“Exactly,” said Umar. “Just like Hindu kings also fought other Hindu kings, and sometimes killed each other — it was about kingdoms, territory, and politics. Not faith.”
There was a long silence at the table. The tension in Arun’s face had eased.
“You know,” he said quietly, “I never thought of it like that. Maybe I was quick to judge.”
Umar smiled. “I understand. We all carry some baggage from the media and stories we hear. But we’re in Finland now — far from the noise. And we’ve got this chance to see each other not as stereotypes, but as people.”
Arun nodded slowly. “You’re right. You’ve always been kind and respectful to me. That speaks louder than any movie.”
“And you’ve been a good friend too,” Umar replied. “Let’s not let the past divide the present. Our job now is to build bridges, not walls.”
That day, something shifted between Arun and Umar — not just friendship, but a deeper respect, a shared understanding, and a quiet commitment to see each other as brothers in humanity.
Moral of the story:
We should never judge a whole community based on the actions of some or the way history is portrayed. Real understanding comes from honest conversations, empathy, and the courage to look beyond stereotypes.

Every time a Salman Khan movie is announced, the excitement automatically kicks in.
The trailer looks promising and expectations rise… but after watching the film, the disappointment feels even worse than before.
It has become a never-ending cycle —
good trailer → huge hype → weak storyline → regret.
Sometimes it makes you wonder: would any sensible actor even sign such scripts?
But then again, Salman Khan doesn’t risk his own money. He knows that even a bad film will cross ₹200+ crore because of his massive fan base. So where is the pressure to improve?
The real question is —
does Salman Khan still want to work with strong storytellers and visionary directors like Prashanth Neel, S.S. Rajamouli, or Sandeep Reddy Vanga?
Or are these directors simply not interested anymore?
Instead, we keep getting films with directors whose past work already tells us what to expect.
Just seeing their names is enough to predict the final result.
If Battle of Girlban turns out to be another disaster, it won’t really matter.
Another bigger disaster will follow.
The producer will recover the money.
The star will move on.
Only the audience will be left disappointed — again.
Still, fans will show up.
So yes…
Get ready for Battle of Girlban.
हिंदी
हर बार जब सलमान ख़ान की कोई नई फ़िल्म अनाउंस होती है, तो अपने आप एक एक्साइटमेंट आ जाती है।
ट्रेलर अच्छा लगता है, उम्मीदें बढ़ जाती हैं… लेकिन फ़िल्म देखने के बाद हर बार निराशा और भी ज़्यादा बढ़ जाती है।
यह एक अंतहीन चक्र बन चुका है —
अच्छा ट्रेलर → ज़बरदस्त हाइप → कमज़ोर कहानी → पछतावा।
कभी-कभी मन में सवाल आता है —
क्या ऐसी स्क्रिप्ट पर कोई समझदार एक्टर साइन भी करता?
लेकिन फिर याद आता है कि सलमान ख़ान अपनी जेब से पैसा नहीं लगाते। उन्हें पता है कि उनकी फ़िल्म चाहे जैसी भी हो, उनका फैनबेस उसे 200 करोड़ के पार पहुँचा ही देगा। तो फिर सुधार करने की ज़रूरत ही कहाँ है?
असली सवाल यह है —
क्या सलमान ख़ान अब भी प्रशांत नील, एस.एस. राजामौली या संदीप रेड्डी वांगा जैसे दमदार डायरेक्टर्स के साथ काम करना चाहते हैं?
या फिर ऐसे डायरेक्टर्स उनके साथ काम करने में दिलचस्पी ही नहीं रखते?
इसके बजाय, बार-बार उन्हीं डायरेक्टर्स के साथ फ़िल्में बन रही हैं जिनका पिछला काम देखकर ही आगे का अंदाज़ा लग जाता है।
उनके नाम से ही फ़िल्म का हाल समझ आ जाता है।
अगर Battle of Girlban भी एक और डिज़ास्टर निकलती है, तो शायद किसी को ज़्यादा फर्क नहीं पड़ेगा।
इसके बाद उससे भी बड़ा डिज़ास्टर आएगा।
प्रोड्यूसर अपना पैसा निकाल लेगा।
स्टार आगे बढ़ जाएगा।
और दर्शक… फिर से निराश होंगे।
फिर भी, लोग फ़िल्म देखने जाएँगे।
तो हाँ —
Battle of Girlban के लिए तैयार रहिए।

People keep calling it a “remake” or “copy-paste,” but let’s not forget the original Champions was a Spanish film, later adapted into Arabic, German, and English. Now, Aamir Khan brings it to Hindi — and if you know his work, you know the kind of depth and commitment he brings.

Let’s move past the remake debate. Every version so far has been beautifully done. Just book your ticket and experience a story that will make you laugh, cry, and see the world through the eyes of those with autism and Down syndrome. Discover their normal.

I feel like this is a movie that everyone in today's time should watch, because our body is not something that is made easily. It takes many parts coming together to form just one complete body. That’s why we are so valuable.

Sometimes in life, even small things can make us feel discouraged, and we start to think that life is meaningless. But when we see how much effort, how many details, and how much time it takes just to form one body, we begin to understand our true worth.

The message shown in this film is very important. That’s why I encourage you to watch it.

I've some suggestions for the makers of this movie which may apply for even upcoming movies of Stree Universe.

1. Firstly, movie should've been a bit shorter. Alok should've become Betal in the initial half an hour. 

2. Dose of love was okay since love was the most important part of this movie but then it fails to land bcoz there isn't any scene that wreches your heart.
Death of Alok should've felt heavier. Rather it seemed as if it just happened. 

3. Fight of Alok and Yakshan should've been a longer one bcoz that was the only good part of the movie but it lasted for hardly 2-3 minutes. If you're building up such a strong villain then let him cook. 

4. Also, what was Yakshasan's character doing? It was cheap comedy throughout which didn't land at all. Rathet it should've been a total gruesome character. It's not that difficult to show such a character without being A rated. Watch Marvel for the same.

5. The only good thing was setting up Bhediya and Thama properly for the next movie and I hope you guys bring out your A game in that. 

6. Overall, a brilliant movie that failed to have an impact due to poor direction and carelessly written cringe dialogues.

For future movies:-
1. Keep script tighter without unnecessary efforts of forced comedy.
2. Keep fight scenes longer bcoz that's what audience expects. 
3. Put better efforts into dialogue writing which could make us feel the weight and depth of the said dialogues.

Instead, we are treated to yet another lecture on “creativity” — a term Harsha continues to redefine as “take an existing film, add slow-mo swagger, sprinkle brooding background score, and pray the audience mistakes inertia for intensity.”

For years, his formula has been clear:

Remake a story that already worked

Replace depth with elevation shots and attitude

Confuse volume for emotion

Package déjà-vu as innovation

It’s cinematic cosplay — glossy, muscular, postured… and hollow enough to echo.

Visionary directors push boundaries. Harsha pushes filters and fog machines.

There is only so much slo-mo a script can carry before the story collapses under the sheer weight of its own self-importance — and Bhimaa and Baaghi 4 proved that in 4K clarity.

Style with substance is cinema.
Style without substance is a two-hour perfume commercial with fight scenes.

Until Harsha learns the difference, the audience’s patience — much like his scripts — will continue to run out halfway through.

Kesari 2 - More than a film it’s a wake up call! 

I was stunned, frozen to my seat from the first frame to the last. My eyes didn’t even flinch once. Kesari 2 didn’t feel like a movie — it felt like a punch to the gut, a scream echoing through history. It was an experience that grips your soul. The intensity, the sacrifice, the sheer will of the characters didn’t let me breathe easy and honestly, it shouldn’t have.

When I got home and heard about the latest terror attacks in Kashmir, my blood was boiling. Are we truly independent? The answer didn’t feel like a yes. If we’re alive today, it’s only because of the unimaginable sacrifices made by those who were slaughtered like animals—without mercy, without justice. Even today, if you visit Jallianwala Bagh you see blood stains on the walls. You can almost hear the cries of babies—2 to 4 months old. It shakes you to your core just to imagine it… and they lived it.

And in the middle of all that darkness, one voice rose. One spark lit up. A 12-year-old boy named Pargat Singh. He opened the eyes of Sankaran Nair. He uncovered the truth of Jallianwala Bagh. And he became a martyr in the process.
More than Sankaran Nair or Dilreet Gill, I want to salute Pargat Singh. Because if it wasn’t for him, we might never have known the real truth behind Jallianwala Bagh. We would’ve continued living in the shadows of the lie that bastard Dyer created.

Kesari 2 doesn’t just tell a story it hits us in the chest. It shakes ours beliefs. It reminds us that our freedom came at a price paid in blood, and that price is still being paid in different ways even today. It’s not just worth watching—it’s necessary. This isn’t just a film. It’s a wake-up call. Watch it—and feel every second of it. It was indeed the BESTEST historical movie I’ve ever watched in my life!

Such utter distortion of history and disgrace to shadow real heroes of independence should be crime. Creating a fictional hero who brought General dyer and Lt. Governor o'dwyer to justice in a trial that never actually happened is so insensitive distortion of history, it shadows the efforts and sentiments of the people of Punjab specifically. The Ghadarites and others. 

The film then flies into some la la land of fantasy. It makes Sankaran Nair team up with a local lawyer to file a case of ‘genocide’ against General Dyer in a local court.

General Dyer was never tried in any court for genocide. In October 1919, the British asked the Hunter Commission to examine some recent ‘disturbances’ in India. The Commission also enquired into the conduct of General Dyer and his claims that he had asked his troops to fire because he feared unrest, anarchy and violence.

Three Indians were part of the Hunter Committee. Sankaran Nair was not one of them. On the basis of the findings of the Committee, General Dyer was relieved of his command in 1920. He died in England, denying all through that he had made a mistake.

Sankaran Nair was a member of the Viceroy’s Executive Council–the precursor to the Indian cabinet–till July 23, 1919. As a member of the council, he agreed to the imposition of Martial Law in Punjab. After his resignation, he joined the then Secretary of State, Edwin Montagu’s council on January 2, 1920

In 1922, many months after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, the findings of the Hunter Commission, and the transfer of Dyer from India, while serving the Indore state as its Diwan, Sankaran Nair wrote a book ‘Gandhi and Anarchy’, a critique of Mahatma Gandhi’s civil disobedience movement. In this book, he “implied the Punjab atrocities were committed with O’Dwyer’s full knowledge and approval.” Michael O’Dwyer was the Lt Governor of Punjab when the massacre took place. General Dyer was the officer who ordered the firing.

O’Dwyer sued Nair for libel and sought an apology. When Nair refused, O’Dwyer took the case to the King’s Bench in London (slightly different from a legal bench).

In the end, Nair lost the case with just one member of the jury favouring him. For his brave fight, Nair was hailed as a hero, and his fight earned him a place in the martyr’s gallery at the Jallianwala Bagh.

The release of Kesari Chapter 2 shows the ongoing exploitation of Sikh history by Bollywood. Jallianwala Bagh, where Sikh families gathered in peace and faced bullets on Vaisakhi, is used here as a background for a story that has little to do with the people who suffered. Sikh lives and voices are treated as material for emotional scenes, while the Sikh spirit that rose from that ground is erased. Bollywood is not engaged in remembrance. It is engaged in extracting whatever it can from Sikh pain to manufacture nationalist entertainment.

Jallianwala Bagh was a direct assault on the Sikh community during one of the holiest days of the Khalsa tradition. The massacre shaped the character of Sikh resistance for the century that followed. In Kesari Chapter 2, this reality is pushed to the side. A Malayali lawyer’s personal awakening is placed at the center while Sikh bodies lie anonymous in the background. There is no trace of the language, spirit, or endurance that defines Sikh history. The massacre is flattened into a generic national tragedy to feed Bollywood’s needs without telling the truth about who stood and who fell.

Bollywood collects Sikh imagery and drapes it over North Indian nationalist fantasy. The casting of Akshay Kumar, who could not even stand with Sikh farmers during a globally historic protest, only underlines the pattern. When Sikh elders sat through the winter fighting for their survival, he chose to side with the government narrative and asked for silence instead of support. Now he returns to use Sikh blood to sell tickets. It is the commercial extraction of another people’s memory for profit.

Sikh suffering does not belong to Bollywood. Sikh blood is not a tool to decorate courtroom dramas and nationalist cinema. Jallianwala Bagh is sacred Sikh ground. Sikhs do not require Bollywood to remember them or misrepresent their history for profit.

😂This movie is a classic example of taking a historical backdrop and turning it into an exaggerated, agenda-driven narrative.General Reginald Dyer was never put on trial for the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

The British government formed the Hunter Commission (1919), which criticized his actions and forced him to retire, but he was never criminally prosecuted. He later suffered a stroke and died in 1927, long before any fictional courtroom scenario.

Michael O’Dwyer, the Lieutenant-Governor of Punjab during the massacre, was also never tried by the British government.

The only major legal case connected to these figures was when Michael O’Dwyer sued C. Sankaran Nair in the London High Court over statements in Nair’s book “Gandhi and Anarchy”, where Nair held O’Dwyer responsible for the massacre.and Nair lost that case.The irony is that Sankaran Nair was actually a critic of Gandhi, yet the film seems to twist history in a way that aligns with today’s political trend of undermining Gandhi’s legacy.

So yes — it’s historically inaccurate, politically motivated, and distorts real events to push a narrative rather than tell the truth.😂

Once again, it’s time to witness Kantara on the big screen — an experience worth every moment.

Lokesh kanagaraj movies day by day📈

Recently watched Coolie, I actually liked this movie. 
1. Had a good blend of characters. 
2. Reminisce Loki Ana's Maanagaram handling of its actors and screenplay. 
3. Some noteworthy stunts. Upendra Sir was brought in well with a superb BGM. 
4. Colour themes used in movie apt. Saturated choices in hostel blends.
5. Shruthi proves she is organic to any given screenplay.
6. Simon, Kalyani, Dahaa all rocked. Dayal sizzled.
7. Loki fans will understand his style of movie making and I feel Coolie was justified @Loki style.
8. Anirudh Ana songs and BGM fit well.
9. Devaraj looked awesome for me. 

Some afterthought for improvement. 
1. The very idea of roasting bodies could have been substituted with a "scientific" concept as the handling of the devices looked very straight forward and don't convince why the thugs could not have done it themselves. 
2. Though may appear cliche, uniting Preethi with Devaraj would have been better. Or at the very least, silently suggest that Preethi knew Deva was her father.
3. The chemistry between Deva and Rajashekar didn't quite click. Perhaps more visuals and screentime required.
4. When we talk about action sequences, I would appreciate some gun sequences using heavy machinery i.e. Kaithi style. It would have packed a punch. 
5. These mid story flash backs i.e. young Simon disrupts movie's momentum, either its best in the beginning or a short recap like post credit scenes. 

Just some thoughts, Loki Ana and team, vazhtugal. Thumbs up from me. Loved the movie. ❤

How could a young girl stay hidden during a terrible war and still have so much hope?
Anne Frank was a Jewish girl who lived during World War II. When the nazis started hurting jewish people, Anne and her family had to go into hiding. While she was hiding, Anne wrote in her diary about her life, feelings, and everything happening around her. her diary showed how scary and unfair that time was, but it also showed how strong and hopeful she was. Even today  people still read her story and learn from her bravery
 After learning about Anne Frank’s early life  important accomplishments, and impact on the world it is clear that she is an important person in history. 
Anne franks early life shows what kind of person she was before the war changed everything.
Anne Frank was born on June 12, 1929, in Frankfurt, Germany. She lived with her mom, dad, and older sister Margot. When Anne was still young, her family moved to Amsterdam because life in Germany was becoming dangerous for Jewish families. Anne was a normal kid in many ways, but she was also very thoughtful and loved to write. She liked sharing her feelings and ideas, which is one reason her diary became so important later. In her diary, Anne wrote, “I hope I will be able to confide everything to you” (Frank). This shows that writing helped her express herself and deal with her thoughts. Anne’s early life was important because it helped shape the girl the world would later remember
One of anne franks biggest achievement was her diary witch helped people understand what life was like during the holocaust .
Anne Frank may have been young, but her writing became famous around the world. While she was hiding with her family, she wrote in her diary almost like she was talking to a friend. Her diary shared her thoughts, fears, and hopes during a very hard time. Anne once wrote, “Paper has more patience than people” (Frank). This shows that writing helped her feel understood when she could not talk freely to others. She also wrote, “I want to go on living even after my death” (Frank). That quote is important because her words really did live on after she died. Anne’s diary became one of the most well-known books from World War II, and it helped many people learn from her story
Anne frank had a big inpact on the world because her diary helped people understand the pain of the holocaust in a personal way.
Even though Anne Frank was just a young girl, her words ended up reaching millions of people. Her diary showed what life was like for a Jewish family hiding during World War II. It helped people see that the Holocaust was not just history, but something real that happened to real families. Anne once wrote, “In spite of everything, I still believe that people are really good at heart” (Frank). This quote is important because it shows how hopeful she stayed, even during such a terrible time. Her diary has been read in schools all over the world and has taught many people about courage, hope, and kindness. Because of Anne Frank, people still remember what happened and why it should never happen again.
Anne frank life shows why she is still such a important person in history.
Her early life, her diary, and her impact on the world all help people understand why her story matters. She went through very hard times, but she still shared her thoughts and feelings through writing. Her diary taught people about the Holocaust in a personal way. Anne Frank deserves to be remembered because her words still teach people about courage, hope, and the importance of remembering the past

Imagine being promised a blockbuster thunderbolt, but what you get is more like your neighbor’s firecracker that fizzles out before the “Happy Independence Day” echo fades. That’s Coolie.

The film bills itself as a gritty union-leader-turned-hero saga—but with a star-studded cast and booming budget of ₹350–400 crore, it feels like the masala was forgotten in the pot. It tries to juggle plot threads like a clown juggling fire torches—light-hearted in intent, but mostly leaving you singed and underwhelmed.

First half? Highlands of spice. Rajinikanth tries to carry the weight like a seasoned port worker, and the opening scenes almost stick. But post-interval, it's more of a slow slog through the suppression of logic. The crime plot? Less Underworld noir, more Underwhelming snore. The action sometimes feels like an overzealous trailer edit—flashy but hollow.

Worse, the screenplay keeps introducing twists like they’re freebies at a roadside stall—one too many, and you just lose the taste. Even Soubin Shahir tries to inject fun, but ends up stranded like a fan missing a firecracker’s final burst. 

Punchy dialogue? More like punch-drunk confusion. Music by Anirudh is flashy, sure—but feels a bit like trying to jazz up bland food with too much garnish. No matter how shiny the decorations, you’re still eating stale dishes.

In short: Coolie is a high-budget, star-loaded can that wants to explode—but forgets the fuse.

Rating: 0.5/5 – A film so overhyped it feels like being promised firework, but getting a damp matchstick instead.

In that sense, watching Lokah Chapter 1: Chandra has been a dream come true. Bhoot Bangla (2026) Review
Bhoot Bangla was extremely disappointing and honestly gave me a headache by the end of it. The movie seemed like it was trying very hard to recreate the charm and success of Bhool Bhulaiyaa-style horror comedy, but it failed badly in execution.
The dialogues were weak and poorly written, with very few memorable moments. Instead of being funny or engaging, most scenes felt forced and dull. The film also failed to properly utilize talented actors like Rajpal Yadav, who could have added much more value if given stronger scenes and better comic timing.
The songs were forgettable and unnecessary, adding no real impact to the story. The climax was one of the weakest parts of the film—poorly written, predictable, and completely unsatisfying.
On the technical side, the CGI and VFX were below average and looked cheap in many scenes, which reduced the horror-comedy effect even further. The plot moved very slowly, making the movie feel unnecessarily stretched and boring. Even the cinematography lacked creativity and failed to create the spooky atmosphere the film needed.
Overall, Bhoot Bangla turned out to be a badly executed attempt at horror comedy with poor writing, weak visuals, and wasted performances. Definitely not worth the time.

Watched Peddi and came out more frustrated than disappointed because this felt like a movie with huge potential that never decided what it wanted to be.

My biggest issue was the lack of focus. In a 3-hour film, why try to fit 3 different sports and make the hero succeed across multiple levels? Instead of creating one strong sports journey and making us emotionally invest in it, the movie kept adding new tracks and diluted the impact.

Ram Charan is shown doing everything—making jaggery, playing cricket, wrestling, running despite injury, winning medals—and after a point it stopped feeling inspiring and started feeling overloaded. A great sports drama makes you root for one difficult journey. Here it felt like the screenplay kept changing lanes before anything fully landed.

What disappointed me most is that Ram Charan clearly put in tremendous effort. You can see the commitment in the physical performance, fights and dance sequences. But effort alone cannot replace strong writing. Many dances were edited or choreographed so fast that the moments didn’t stay with you.

The action portions also felt weak. Usually mass movies build hero elevation through memorable payoff moments, but here the fights felt repetitive and surprisingly ordinary. The hero struggled through long fight sequences but the movie never converted that struggle into emotionally satisfying moments.

Jagapathi Babu’s character felt underused too. He has the screen presence to carry emotional weight, but here the role felt reduced and never created the impact it could have.

Janhvi Kapoor’s character and political angle also felt disconnected. Her father’s election setup looked important initially, but by the climax the conflict and alliances didn’t feel emotionally earned. The love story itself barely felt developed. There wasn’t enough chemistry or progression between the lead pair to make it memorable.

The heroine’s presentation also didn’t work for me—not because of the actor, but because of the writing and visual treatment. Instead of building authenticity and depth into the character, the movie seemed more interested in adding glamour where it wasn’t necessary.

Another thing I couldn’t understand: why have separate conflicts and villains around different sports? One track for cricket, another for wrestling, politics somewhere else, romance somewhere else. Why not choose one sport, one central conflict and one strong antagonist? It would have made the story tighter and easier to connect with.

Too many characters entered and exited without purpose. Supporting roles didn’t leave much impression and even some simple dialogues didn’t feel natural or easy to connect with.

For me, Peddi tried to be a sports drama, village drama, political drama, romance, mass entertainer and action film all at once—and ended up not excelling in any one of them.

This felt less like a complete movie and more like a collection of ideas competing with each other.

“Arun did not die — he became a symbol of the spirit of the Indian soldier.”
— Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw (reported remark on his bravery)

My grandfather was a tank commander and was martyred in the 1971 war — a great artist as well. Though I never met him, I feel his spirit lives through my art. Every stroke I paint is a tribute to him. The movie Ikkis is not just a film — it’s for families like ours, who carry the legacy and pride of 1971 in their hearts.

I am writing this complete story after receiving so many comments.

My grandfather served in the Deccan Horse regiment. During a fierce battle, while he was in his tank, a call for help came from another tank operator who was badly injured and needed immediate medical aid.

My grandfather wanted to help him, but his fellow tank members advised him not to open the hatch as there was heavy firing from both sides. But how could he leave a comrade behind? A Rajput by blood never abandons someone in need.

He opened the hatch, returned fire at the enemy, and in the crossfire, he was martyred while saving another soldier’s life.
He left behind four children — three daughters and one son — and a brave, warm-hearted widow at the age of just 35.

His story reminds me that courage runs in the blood, and sacrifice builds the legacy.

Just imagine the temperament of a 21 year old boy who was hit by shells in his face before he destroyed 3 tanks, then cleaned his wounded face blood dripping through his  eyes then he destroyed 2 more tanks. Then died because his tank was also hit by enemy tanks. Ultimate courage and sacrifice for country 🇮🇳. Paramveer chakra.

Just for information -
Many Indian soldiers have died at age 21, with prominent examples including Second Lieutenant Arun Khetarpal, a Param Vir Chakra recipient in the 1971 war, and Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat, a Maha Vir Chakra awardee from the 1962 Sino-Indian War, both known for immense bravery at a young age. Ekkis disappoints deeply by failing to portray the story with honesty or historical responsibility. Instead of engaging with the complexities of Bharat’s past, the film falls back on tired, old Bollywood-style “Aman ki Asha” messaging that feels more like propaganda than storytelling.
This one-sided idealism ignores hard realities and oversimplifies history. Peace slogans may sound good on screen, but history cannot be rewritten to fit a comfortable narrative. The film seems unwilling to acknowledge that such “Aman ki Asha” was never mutual, and that Bharat’s experiences were far more complex and painful.
Bharat has always believed in “Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam”—the world as one family—but that belief should not require denying truth or glossing over facts. Cinema has a responsibility to reflect reality, not escape it. Sadly, Erik’s chooses convenience over courage, making it an unsatisfying and misleading watch.
